title: Early Childhood in India
summary: The period from birth to six years is a time of rapid development; care and stimulation are critical in the first three years. Children are vulnerable and need care, protection and chances to realise their potential. Legally, children are those under 18. Each culture defines childhood in its own way; childhood is generally a time of playing, learning, socialising and exploring.
## Status of young children in India

Children are the future of the nation. India is a multi-cultural, pluralistic society; Census 2011 counted about 158.8 million children aged 0–6 (13.12% of the population). Infant mortality, longevity and literacy are determinants of the Human Development Index.

NFHS-4 (2015–16): child sex ratio rose from 914 to 919; Infant Mortality Rate (deaths of children under one year per 1000 live births) fell from 57 to 41; Under-five Mortality Rate fell to 50; women married before 18 fell from 47.4% to 26.8%; 35.8% of children under five are underweight and 38.4% stunted; 68.8% of children attend school. Child mortality = deaths of children under five per 1000 live births. Lack of resources leads to ill health, high-density living and unhygienic conditions; better sanitation, clean water and medical care explain the fall in IMR.

Maternal mortality is death of a woman during pregnancy or within 42 days of its end due to its complications; India cut its maternal mortality ratio from 556 (1990) to 130 (2016). Exclusive breastfeeding is advised for the first six months; local ICDS centres provide primary health care and immunisation. The Maternity Benefit Amendment Act, 2017 makes childcare facilities at workplaces mandatory. Girls face denial of health care and nutrition and early dropout (literacy: girls 65.5%, boys 82.1%).

Diversity rests on physical, social, cultural, linguistic, religious and ethnic factors. Caste has been a source of discrimination and lowers children's self-worth; Scheduled Tribes, often in remote forest areas, face exclusion or 'adverse inclusion'. India is secular and multi-religious; the Constitution forbids discrimination on grounds of religion. Family configurations range from nuclear to extended; children of widowed or single women, adopted children, children with disabilities and the 4–6 million children affected by migration face special challenges, such as denial of education during seasonal migration.
## Impact of early childhood on later life

Development is shaped by nature (genes) and nurture (family, care, education, environment). 'Use it or lose it' and 'serve and return' stress responsive care and stimulation. Children who face poverty, neglect or abuse early are more likely to have social, emotional, behavioural, school-adjustment and mental-health problems, and may repeat poor parenting as adults; sensitive parenting, family and community support and good childcare reduce these effects.

Heredity (height, eye colour, some aptitudes, inherited diseases) and environment (stimulation, loving relationships, good school); exercise; sex of the child; nutrition (protein deficiency causes stunting, overeating obesity); familial influence (attachment, 'it takes a village to raise a child'); geographical influences (neighbourhood, parks, libraries); socio-economic status (long-term poverty leads to poor attention and more delays). Helen Keller shows how nurture can overcome limits.

Hygiene (self and environment), sanitation (safe disposal of excreta and sewage to stop faecal-oral spread), nutrition (Recommended Dietary Allowance; malnutrition = under-nutrition — stunting, wasting, underweight, micronutrient deficiency — or overweight), immunisation (polio eliminated) and maternal health (healthy mothers have healthy babies; at least 20% of the disease burden of under-fives is linked to maternal health).

Article 14 equality before law; 15 no discrimination (special provisions for women and children); 17 untouchability abolished; 21A free and compulsory education for 6–14 years; 24 no child below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work; 39 children not abused or forced by economic necessity into unsuitable work, and given chances to develop in freedom and dignity; 42 maternity relief; 45 free and compulsory education until 14 (now early childhood care); 46 educational and economic interests of weaker sections, SCs and STs; 47 raising nutrition, standard of living and public health; 51A(k) parents' duty to educate children of 6–14.

Child-rearing practices are culturally grounded ways in which parents and caregivers bring up a child. At birth and in the first year the child is at the greatest risk of mortality, so many customs surround birth; a period of confinement lets the mother recover and bond, but may keep her from medical care. The support the mother gets from family and community decides the quality of care.

vsa: What is meant by religious plurality? How does it affect children?

Religious plurality means many religions — Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Jainism, Islam, Christianity and tribal religions — coexist in secular India. Religion shapes children's dress, food, customs and festivals and their sense of identity, so schools should know these practices and connect home festivities with school.
How does the socio-economic status of a family affect a child's development?

It decides the family's means and access to resources. Well-off families can afford better schools and materials; poverty often comes with illiteracy, poor childcare and less constructive beliefs. Children in long-term poverty show poor attention span, poor retention and more developmental delays.
Explain the influence of maternal health on the health of a child.

Healthy children are born to healthy mothers, and infants depend on breast milk for the first six months. At least 20% of the disease burden of under-fives is linked to maternal health and nutrition and care at delivery; a baby whose mother dies at birth is less likely to survive.

Both are signs of under-nutrition. Stunting is low height for age, showing long-term malnutrition and lack of stimulation; wasting is low weight for height, showing recent or acute lack of food. NFHS-4 found 38.4% of under-fives stunted.

Practices grounded in cultural patterns and beliefs that parents and caregivers adopt for the care and upbringing of a child — for example, birth customs, confinement of the mother, feeding and weaning ceremonies. They depend on the child's age and the health and nutritional risks the child faces.
sa: What is the impact of early childhood on subsequent life?

Early childhood is a sensitive period shaped by nature and nurture, when the brain grows fastest; children 'use it or lose it' and benefit from 'serve and return' interaction. A stimulating, caring, healthy environment gives lasting gains. Adversity — poverty, neglect, abuse, frequent illness — leads to social, emotional, behavioural and school-adjustment problems, even mental-health problems or delinquency, and such adults may repeat poor parenting. Sensitive parenting, family and community support and good childcare can moderate these effects.

or: What is the constitutional view of childhood in India?

The Constitution treats children's survival, development and protection as rights and duties: Article 14 equality before law; 15 no discrimination and special provisions for children; 21A free and compulsory education for 6–14; 24 no child below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work; 39 children not abused or forced into unsuitable work and given chances to develop in freedom and dignity; 45 free and compulsory education; 46 interests of weaker sections; 47 nutrition and public health; 51A(k) parents' duty to educate their children.

sa: How does maternal mortality affect child survival and development?

Maternal mortality is the death of a woman from complications of pregnancy and childbirth (or within 42 days). A baby whose mother dies at birth is less likely to survive, and children who lose their mothers are ten times more likely to die within two years. It depends on the mother's age, health and wellbeing; early marriage (before 18) makes robust motherhood less likely and raises IMR.

or: Why is breastfeeding considered important for the health of both mother and child?

Breast milk is a complete, wholesome food for the newborn for the first six months and protects against infection, lowering illness and deaths; it also gives touch, comfort and bonding. NFHS-4 notes early breastfeeding within an hour of delivery. For the mother it builds the bond with the baby, and communities have customs and foods to support lactation.

sa: How do families need to accommodate children with special conditions, and what challenges do they face?

Children with disabilities are among the most excluded; many do not complete primary education. Families must meet their special requirements, which often need extra care, time, money and therapy from parents, and help them join mainstream schools. Siblings and other children need counselling to understand differences and reach out with empathy.

or: What are the challenges faced by migrant children, particularly those of families employed in the unorganised sector?

An estimated 4–6 million children are affected by migration. Their families face exclusion from basic services, exploitative work (no minimum wages, no social security), gender-based wage discrimination and denial of maternity rights and childcare. Seasonal migration disrupts schooling and often denies the child's right to education.

sa: How does India's multi-cultural society contribute to diverse social environments for children?

India is a pluralistic society where people of different religions, languages, castes, tribes and economic backgrounds live together, across varied regions (Himalayas, plains, deserts, coasts). These differences in beliefs, resources, food, dress and customs give children very different experiences of childhood; some groups are disadvantaged by caste discrimination, poverty or remoteness.

or: What factors contribute to the poor health and living conditions of children in India?

Uneven distribution of economic resources, lack of access and awareness lead to ill health, high-density living and unhygienic conditions. Other causes are malnutrition (stunting, wasting), infection and lack of sanitation and clean water, poor maternal health and early marriage, and gender bias against girls in health care and nutrition.

la: Briefly explain the factors affecting childhood.

Heredity: genes from parents decide height, body structure, eye colour, hair texture, partly intelligence and aptitudes, and some diseases. Environment: physical and psychological stimulation, positive modelling and loving relationships build skills and aspiration. Exercise: play builds muscle strength and bone mass and helps children reach milestones. Sex of the child: boys and girls grow at different rates, especially near puberty. Nutrition: a balanced diet is needed for growth and repair; protein deficiency causes stunting, overeating obesity. Familial influence: consistent, responsive adults build attachment; stress, neglect or too much control harm development. Geographical influences: neighbourhood parks, libraries and peers shape interests. Socio-economic status: poverty limits access and long-term poverty causes more delays. Adequate rest and sleep also matter.

la: Describe the factors influencing children's health.

Hygiene: personal (washing hands after the toilet, brushing teeth, bathing, clean clothes, cut nails, covering mouth and nose) and environmental (no stagnant water, covered drinking water). Sanitation: safe treatment and disposal of excreta and sewage to stop faecal-oral spread of disease. Nutrition: a balanced diet of proteins, carbohydrates, fats, minerals, vitamins, fibre and water as per the RDA; malnutrition shows as stunting, wasting, underweight, micronutrient deficiency or obesity. Immunisation: vaccines (BCG, OPV, DPT, measles, MMR, etc.) on a fixed schedule protect from infections, as with the elimination of polio. Maternal health: healthy mothers have healthy babies; good nutrition in pregnancy and two years after birth gives children the best chance to survive.
